title: 3-Read Friday #110: Responsible AI, LLMs Mimicking Students, and Screen Time in Schools
author: Craig Barton, Simon Woodhead, Bibi Groot
summary: EEDI's weekly roundup, curated by Craig Barton with contributions from Chief Data Scientist Simon Woodhead and Chief Impact Officer Bibi Groot, covers three items at the intersection of AI, assessment, and classroom technology. Woodhead highlights Burstein et al.'s paper on the Duolingo English Test, which proposes a novel psychometric framework for assessing non-traditional response types (dialogues, confidence levels, explanations) that conventional psychometrics cannot handle. Groot flags Borchers, Vie, and Azevedo's finding that GPT-4.1 simulates student think-aloud reasoning poorly: LLM outputs are too long, too confident, and too coherent compared to real struggling students, a limitation the underlying arXiv paper attributes to training data drawn from expert-like solutions rather than the fragmented, affect-laden reasoning of actual novices. Barton's own pick, Zach Groshell's piece on screen time, argues that blanket bans dodge the harder question of what students are actually doing on screens. Together the three items press the same underlying point: responsible use of AI and technology in education depends on confronting its precise limitations rather than adopting sweeping rules for or against it.
points: Traditional psychometric methods were built for simple, standardized assessment formats; as AI enables richer data (dialogues, confidence levels, explanations), Duolingo's approach offers a replicable model for validating non-traditional assessment.

GPT-4.1's simulations of student think-aloud reasoning are systematically too long, confident, and coherent compared to real novice learners, a gap the original arXiv study ties directly to LLM training data being dominated by expert-authored, affect-free solutions.

The Borchers et al. finding carries a design implication for AI tutoring: a model that cannot faithfully represent how a struggling student thinks risks fading instructional scaffolding before the student is genuinely ready.

Groshell's argument reframes the screen-time debate: banning screens outright is a category error that discards well-designed instructional tools because activity-based teaching, not the technology itself, has misused them.

Responsible AI in education requires pairing better assessment frameworks for non-traditional response types with more realistic models of learner cognition; tools built without both risk misrepresenting the students they are meant to serve.
quotes: Eedi has always been dedicated to novel forms of assessment that elicit students' misconceptions. We started with diagnostic MCQs, collected students' explanations and confidence levels, and are now collecting their dialogues with a tutor.

Normally you would turn to psychometrics to map these student behaviours to cognitive insights, but traditional psychometric methods can only be applied to simple assessment types. In this article, Duolingo uncovers its novel approach to reliable, validated assessments outside the traditional setting.

Borchers, Vie and Azevedo asked GPT-4.1 to simulate novice learners thinking aloud, and the LLM simulations of "learner utterances" were much too long, confident, and coherent (in comparison to think-aloud data from real students).

LLMs are trained on expert-authored text; they don't naturally grasp messy, emotional, half-formed reasoning. For anyone building AI tutoring, this matters: if the model can't faithfully represent how a struggling student thinks, it might fade scaffolding too prematurely.

Zach tackles the divisive topic of screen times in schools with his trademark nuance. He argues that banning screens wholesale dodges the harder question of what students are actually doing on them, and risks discarding scalable, well-designed instructional tools because activity-based teaching has misused them.

Although GPT-4.1 generates fluent and contextually appropriate continuations, its reasoning is systematically over-coherent, verbose, and less variable than human think-alouds. These effects intensify with a richer problem-solving context during prompting.
